Messages.Author: Luis P. Duarte
Messages.Body:
1. Can i block another player Bum's Rush directed to a minion controlled
by my predator?

2. And can i block a bleed directed to my predator?

3. Can i block a PA called by a minion controlled by a player that is not
my predator nor my prey?

4. If a minion controlled by a player that is not my predator nor my prey
is trying to burn an Haven Uncovered on him, can "i" try to block it?

5. Can i play a Sudden Reversal to forbid another Master-out-of-turn
played by another player? And can a third player play another Sudden
Reversal to forbid mine?

Thanx!
.- Luis....@ip.pt

Messages.Author: Dhar...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
Luis P. Duarte wrote:
> 1. Can i block another player Bum's Rush directed to a minion controlled
> by my predator?
>
> 2. And can i block a bleed directed to my predator?
>
> 3. Can i block a PA called by a minion controlled by a player that is not
> my predator nor my prey?

With Eagle's Sight or Anneke you can. Otherwise, no.

> 4. If a minion controlled by a player that is not my predator nor my prey
> is trying to burn an Haven Uncovered on him, can "i" try to block it?

Burning a Haven Uncovered is a (D) action. It doesn't matter if you're
the predator or prey....only if you're the player who played it. Again,
Eage's Sight overcomes that hindrance.

> 5. Can i play a Sudden Reversal to forbid another Master-out-of-turn
> played by another player? And can a third player play another Sudden
> Reversal to forbid mine?

Absolutely...as long it's not the current turn of the above three platyers.
I've seen it happen.

Dhar...@yahoo.com wrote:
> Luis P. Duarte wrote:
> > 1. Can i block another player Bum's Rush directed to a minion controlled
> > by my predator?
> >
> > 2. And can i block a bleed directed to my predator?
> >
> > 3. Can i block a PA called by a minion controlled by a player that is not
> > my predator nor my prey?
>
> With Eagle's Sight or Anneke you can. Otherwise, no.

Well, Enzo Giovanni also has card text regarding the latter case, but right:
barring explicit card text, only ready untapped minions controlled by
the target of a directed action can attempt to block that action. And only
ready untapped minions controlled by the predator or prey of the acting
minion's controller can attempt to block an undirected action (and all PAs
are undirected actions). [6.2.2.1]

> > 4. If a minion controlled by a player that is not my predator nor my prey
> > is trying to burn an Haven Uncovered on him, can "i" try to block it?
>
> Burning a Haven Uncovered is a (D) action. It doesn't matter if you're
> the predator or prey....only if you're the player who played it. Again,
> Eage's Sight overcomes that hindrance.

Right. Burning Haven is directed because Haven is still controlled by the
Methuselah who played it (it is a Master card), and any action which targets
another Methuselah's card(s) is directed (at that Methuselah).

>
> > 5. Can i play a Sudden Reversal to forbid another Master-out-of-turn
> > played by another player? And can a third player play another Sudden
> > Reversal to forbid mine?
>
> Absolutely...as long it's not the current turn of the above three platyers.
> I've seen it happen.

Right.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 18 Nov 1998, Luis P. Duarte wrote:

> A tournment situation i saw:
> Player A has a Weenie-Bleed deck and 7 ready vampires.
> Player B (NOT prey or predator of Player A) decides to
> play an Anarchist Uprising, that will not affect his own
> predator and prey. The only affected player is A.

How so? Do you mean that only player A has minions on the table? I
presume you mean that all Methuselahs were affected, but player A
disproportionately so because of the nature of his deck.

> Is this legal? (Not by card rules but by tournment "behavior")

It is legal. What is not legal is collusion. Thus, his behavior is a
problem only to the extent that it constitutes evidence of collusion.

For a great number of reasons, it seems very unlikely that the situation
you describe is real evidence of collusion. Far more likely is that he
designed a weenie-hosing deck in the hope that such decks would be his
opposition, and got stuck with a non-weenie predator and prey. Now he is
simply trying to play the deck he is stuck with.

> (The judge didn't saw this situation but several other players
> said this wasn't a good conduct and player B *couldn't* play
> it because he had no reason to do it)

Maybe he just needed to burn the card. Or maybe he has a Dramatic
Upheaval coming up and plans to switch positions whenever player A's pool
gets low. Maybe he fears that player A will sweep the table and wants to
eliminate him to give himself a chance. Or maybe he's just playing badly.

Unless there is a real reason to suspect that he is hurting player A as
part of a plan to help a 3rd party win (ie.,that he is not in it for
himself), then he can play as he chooses. There is no reason to limit his
options.

> Anyway, the second time player B tried to play another AU,
> player A plays a Delaying Tactics.
> What if player A didn't have a DT?

Even if player A *was* his prey: What if player A had no intercept?

In either case, the vote will be decided by a referendum.

> By the rules you described, player A couldn't try to block the PA,
> although he's the target!

Right (though he is not really the target, technically). This sort of
thin often happens. In a recent JOL game I was "targetted" with
conservative agitation from accross the table to gain vote support from my
prey. There was nothing I could do about it, (except torporize my Prey's
prince on a subsequent round).

Lupus Australis

Player A has a Weenie-Bleed deck and 7 ready vampires.
Player B (NOT prey or predator of Player A) decides to
play an Anarchist Uprising, that will not affect his own
predator and prey. The only affected player is A.

it because he had no reason to do it)

player A plays a Delaying Tactics.
What if player A didn't have a DT?

By the rules you described, player A couldn't try to block the PA,
although he's the target!

Comments?

Thanx!

Messages.Author: Dhar...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
> A tournment situation i saw:
> Player A has a Weenie-Bleed deck and 7 ready vampires.
> Player B (NOT prey or predator of Player A) decides to
> play an Anarchist Uprising, that will not affect his own
> predator and prey. The only affected player is A.
>

> Is this legal? (Not by card rules but by tournment "behavior")

Hell yes, this is legal. The day that tournament "behavior" becomes
subject to ruling is the day I sell all my Jyhad cards.

Part of the strength of voting decks is their ability to strike anywhere
on the table that they want. If I want to strike cross-table with KRC
or CA, that's my perogative.

> (The judge didn't saw this situation but several other players
> said this wasn't a good conduct and player B *couldn't* play
> it because he had no reason to do it)

That's complete bullshit. Nobody wants to over-run by a weenie
horde. If a player bitches about something like this at a tournament
that I run, I'm likely to eject him and tell him to go play Magic: the
Crack Habit with all the rest of the little whining teenagers.
(No...I actually wouldn't, but I can guarantee that I wouldn't be
supportive of that kind of whining)

> Anyway, the second time player B tried to play another AU,
> player A plays a Delaying Tactics.
> What if player A didn't have a DT?

In a word, "Tough"

I don't know what kind of people you play with, but the people who
play Jyhad in this state are adults (average age is about 25 or so)
and are very much aware of the risks of playing a weenie horde.
Anarch Uprisings are one of the few ways to kill a weenie horde
and I'm all for it. Take the good with the bad.

Noal McDonald
